dx: Transposition of the great arteries in a newborn of a mother with diabetes
case: A 1-day-old boy, born at 39 weeks' gestation to a woman with poorly controlled pregestational type 1 diabetes mellitus, develops progressive cyanosis 6 hours after birth. Birth weight is 4.3 kg (9.5 lb). Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 64/min, and blood pressure is 64/40 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 68% on room air (reference 95% to 100%). There is no murmur, and S2 is single and loud. Chest x-ray shows a narrow superior mediastinum with an egg-shaped cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arising from the left ventricle, an intact ventricular septum, a small patent ductus arteriosus, and a small patent foramen ovale. The diagnosis is dextro-transposition of the great arteries.

questions.stem: An intravenous infusion of prostaglandin E1 is started to keep the ductus arteriosus open. Which of the following best explains why this infant's survival depends on open fetal channels?
options: Pulmonary blood flow must bypass an atretic pulmonary valve
Systemic blood flow must bypass a hypoplastic aortic arch
The two circuits run in parallel and need a site of mixing
Ductal flow unloads the right ventricle to prevent its failure
approach: Identify the anatomy: aorta from the right ventricle, pulmonary artery from the left ventricle.
Trace the blood: body blood returns to the body, and lung blood returns to the lungs.
Conclude that oxygen reaches the tissues only where the two circuits mix, through a PDA, ASD, or VSD.
questions.why: In transposition, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. Deoxygenated body blood goes straight back out the aorta, and oxygenated lung blood goes straight back to the lungs. The two circuits run side by side instead of one after the other, so no oxygen reaches the body unless blood crosses between them. A PDA, ASD, or VSD provides that crossing, which is why prostaglandin E1 and often a balloon atrial septostomy keep the infant alive until the arterial switch operation.
whyNot: Ductal dependence for lung blood flow occurs with pulmonary atresia or critical pulmonic stenosis, including severe tetralogy of Fallot. This infant's pulmonary artery arises normally sized from the left ventricle.
Ductal dependence for body blood flow occurs with critical coarctation or hypoplastic left heart syndrome. Here the aorta and its arch are normal in size.
Correct.
The ductus is kept open so that blood can mix. In transposition the right ventricle pumps to the body by design, and unloading it is not the goal.

questions.stem: A balloon atrial septostomy is performed to enlarge the opening between his atria. In a healthy newborn, which of the following changes at birth normally closes this opening?
options: Left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure
Right atrial pressure rises after umbilical cord clamping
Rising arterial PO2 constricts the septum primum
Falling prostaglandin E2 contracts the septum secundum
approach: Name the opening: the foramen ovale, a flap valve that lets blood pass right to left in the fetus.
Ask what reverses the pressure gradient at birth: more pulmonary venous return to the left atrium and less placental return to the right atrium.
Separate this from ductal closure, which depends on oxygen and prostaglandin E2.
questions.why: With the first breaths, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and lung blood flow rises sharply. More blood returns through the pulmonary veins, so left atrial pressure rises. Clamping the cord removes placental return, so right atrial pressure falls. The higher left atrial pressure presses the septum primum against the septum secundum and closes the foramen ovale functionally. Anatomic fusion follows over months and leaves the fossa ovalis.
whyNot: Correct.
Right atrial pressure falls after the cord is clamped, because placental venous return stops. A rise would push the flap open.
Rising PO2 constricts the smooth muscle of the ductus arteriosus. The septum primum is a thin flap that closes by pressure, with no such response to oxygen.
Falling prostaglandin E2 helps close the ductus arteriosus. It has no role in closing the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: Before the septostomy, the infant breathes 100% oxygen by hood for 10 minutes. His oxygen saturation rises only from 68% to 71%. Which of the following best explains this small response?
options: Oxygen diffusion across a thickened alveolar membrane is limited
Fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen with low affinity in the lungs
Low ventilation-perfusion ratios exist in poorly expanded lung units
Systemic venous blood reaches the aorta without passing alveoli
approach: Note the clue: saturation barely rises with 100% O2.
Sort the causes of hypoxemia: low V/Q, diffusion limitation, and hypoventilation correct with O2, while shunt does not.
Match transposition to a right-to-left shunt: body venous blood bypasses the alveoli.
questions.why: Breathing 100% O2 raises PO2 only in blood that passes ventilated alveoli. In transposition, most body venous blood goes from the right ventricle straight into the aorta and never meets alveolar gas, which acts like a large right-to-left shunt. Blood leaving the lungs is already nearly fully saturated, so extra O2 adds little to it. Mixing that blood with the large shunted flow barely changes arterial saturation. A poor rise with 100% O2 (the hyperoxia test) points to cyanotic heart disease rather than lung disease.
whyNot: Diffusion limitation improves well with 100% O2, because the high alveolar PO2 speeds diffusion. This infant's alveolar membranes are normal.
Fetal hemoglobin has a higher O2 affinity than adult hemoglobin, which helps loading in the lungs. It does not explain a poor response to O2.
Low V/Q units improve markedly with 100% O2, because even poorly ventilated alveoli slowly fill with O2. This is how lung disease is told apart from a fixed shunt.
Correct.

questions.stem: The defect began during the fifth week of development, when cells that migrated from the neural folds into the outflow tract built the partition between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Which of the following errors best explains this infant's anatomy?
options: Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Straight, nonspiraling growth of the aorticopulmonary septum
Failure of the truncus arteriosus to divide into two vessels
Incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions of the AV canal
approach: List the facts: two separate great arteries, each from the wrong ventricle.
Recall that neural crest cells build a spiral aorticopulmonary septum.
Choose the error that keeps two vessels but connects them wrongly: failure to spiral.
questions.why: Neural crest cells migrate into the truncus and conus and form the truncal and conal ridges. These ridges normally twist about 180 degrees as they fuse, so the aorta ends up connected to the left ventricle and the pulmonary trunk to the right ventricle. If the septum grows straight down without spiraling, each great artery connects to the wrong ventricle. The result is transposition of the great arteries, which is more common in infants of mothers with diabetes.
whyNot: Anterosuperior shift of the infundibular septum produces tetralogy of Fallot: pulmonic stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The great arteries keep their normal connections.
Correct.
Failed septation leaves a single trunk over a VSD, which is persistent truncus arteriosus. This infant has two separate great arteries.
Endocardial cushion defects cause atrioventricular septal defects, common in Down syndrome. This infant's septum is intact, and the problem lies in the outflow tract.

dx: Eisenmenger syndrome from an unrepaired membranous ventricular septal defect
case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasing shortness of breath with exertion over 2 years. A heart murmur was found when she was 2 years old, but it was never treated. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 84% on room air (reference 95% to 100%). Physical examination shows central cyanosis, digital clubbing, a left parasternal heave, and a loud single S2. No murmur is heard. Hemoglobin is 19.8 g/dL (reference 12 to 16 g/dL), and hematocrit is 60% (reference 36% to 46%). Echocardiography shows a 1.5-cm membranous ventricular septal defect with mostly right-to-left flow and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 105 mm Hg (reference 15 to 30 mm Hg). The diagnosis is Eisenmenger syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the change in the direction of flow across her defect over time?
options: Left ventricular hypertrophy raised systemic ventricular pressure
Arteriolar remodeling raised pulmonary vascular resistance
Secondary polycythemia raised the viscosity of venous blood
Right ventricular dilation lowered right-sided filling pressure
approach: Recall that shunt direction follows the pressure difference between the ventricles.
Ask what made right-sided pressure exceed left-sided pressure: rising pulmonary vascular resistance.
Link that resistance to remodeling of pulmonary arterioles after years of high flow.
questions.why: A large VSD first sends blood left to right, because left ventricular systolic pressure is far higher. The extra flow and pressure injure the pulmonary arterioles, which respond with medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation, and eventually plexiform lesions. Pulmonary vascular resistance rises until right ventricular pressure equals and then exceeds left ventricular pressure. The shunt then reverses, and deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation, causing late cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia.
whyNot: A higher left-sided pressure would increase left-to-right flow. It cannot reverse the shunt.
Correct.
Polycythemia is a response to low arterial O2, driven by erythropoietin. It follows the reversal and does not cause it.
Lower right-sided pressure would favor left-to-right flow. Reversal needs right-sided pressure higher than left-sided pressure.

questions.stem: Her childhood records describe a murmur that was easy to hear at that time. Which of the following best describes the murmur most likely documented at age 2 years?
options: Continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle
Midsystolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border
Late systolic apical murmur preceded by a midsystolic click
Harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
approach: Place the defect: the membranous ventricular septum.
Reason from pressures: the left ventricle exceeds the right through all of systole, so flow is holosystolic.
Place the sound over the ventricular septum: the left lower sternal border.
questions.why: In childhood, left ventricular pressure was much higher than right ventricular pressure through all of systole. Blood jetted across the membranous septum from the start to the end of systole, giving a harsh holosystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border. Many small defects close on their own, while large ones can cause heart failure in infancy. As her pulmonary resistance rose and the ventricular pressures equalized, the jet slowed and the murmur faded, which is why no murmur is heard now.
whyNot: A continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle comes from a patent ductus arteriosus, where aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure in both systole and diastole.
An ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border with a fixed split S2 points to an atrial septal defect. That murmur comes from extra flow across the pulmonic valve.
A midsystolic click with a late systolic apical murmur is mitral valve prolapse, which does not cause a shunt.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her defect lies in the thin upper part of the ventricular septum, the last part of the septum to close, at about the end of the seventh week. Which of the following tissues forms this part of the septum?
options: Endocardial cushion tissue joined to conotruncal ridges
Upward growth of the muscular interventricular septum alone
Fusion of the atrial septum primum with the septum secundum
Myocardium of the bulbus cordis forming the outflow wall
approach: Name the region: the membranous septum, the last part to close.
Recall the tissues that meet to close the interventricular foramen.
Pick the answer that includes endocardial cushion tissue joined to the conotruncal ridges.
questions.why: The muscular septum grows up from the floor of the ventricle but leaves a gap, the interventricular foramen. Tissue from the inferior endocardial cushion closes this gap by joining the conotruncal (aorticopulmonary) ridges and the top of the muscular septum. Because several tissues must meet, this membranous region is the most common site of a VSD. The fused endocardial cushions also divide the atrioventricular canal and help form the mitral and tricuspid valves, so cushion defects in Down syndrome can involve the atrial septum, the ventricular septum, and both AV valves.
whyNot: Correct.
The muscular septum forms the lower, thick part of the septum. Defects there are muscular VSDs, which are less common.
The septum primum and septum secundum form the atrial septum and the foramen ovale. They do not reach the ventricles.
The bulbus cordis forms the smooth outflow parts of the ventricles (conus arteriosus and aortic vestibule). It does not close the interventricular foramen.

questions.stem: Her S2 is single and does not split during inspiration. In a healthy young adult, which of the following best explains the normal splitting of S2 during inspiration?
options: More venous return to the left heart delays aortic closure
Higher systemic afterload during inspiration delays aortic closure
More venous return to the right heart delays pulmonic closure
Slower conduction in the right bundle delays right ventricular systole
approach: Recall the order of S2: A2 before P2.
Ask what inspiration does: more blood to the right heart, a little less to the left.
Conclude that P2 moves later and A2 slightly earlier, widening the split.
questions.why: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, which draws more venous blood into the right heart and lowers pulmonary vascular impedance. The right ventricle ejects a larger volume for longer, so P2 comes later. At the same time, blood pools in the expanding pulmonary veins, left ventricular filling falls slightly, and A2 comes a little earlier. The two sounds separate on inspiration and merge on expiration. In this patient, very high pulmonary artery pressure makes P2 loud and early, so S2 sounds single.
whyNot: Inspiration slightly reduces left ventricular filling, so aortic closure comes a little earlier. A larger left-sided volume would narrow the split.
Systemic afterload does not rise with normal inspiration. A late A2, as in aortic stenosis or left bundle branch block, narrows or reverses the split (paradoxical splitting).
Correct.
Right bundle branch block delays right ventricular systole and widens the split in both phases of breathing. A healthy adult has normal conduction.

dx: Isolated coarctation of the aorta with rib notching in a young man with a bicuspid aortic valve
case: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician for a preparticipation sports examination. He reports cramping in both calves after running about 1 km. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 168/94 mm Hg in the right arm and 164/92 mm Hg in the left arm. Femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with the radial pulses. An early systolic ejection click is heard at the apex, and a systolic murmur is heard over the back between the scapulae. Chest x-ray shows notching of the lower borders of the posterior third to eighth ribs. Echocardiography shows a bicuspid aortic valve with normal function. CT angiography shows a discrete narrowing of the aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. The diagnosis is coarctation of the aorta.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the direction of blood flow in the vessels that cause his rib notching?
options: Descending aorta to intercostal arteries, then to the internal thoracic arteries
Intercostal veins to the azygos vein, then to the superior vena cava
Pulmonary arteries to bronchial arteries, then to the descending aorta
Internal thoracic to intercostal arteries, then to the descending aorta
approach: Locate the block: just past the left subclavian artery, so pressure is high above and low below.
Find the arterial route from subclavian branches to the aorta below the block: internal thoracic to anterior and then posterior intercostal arteries.
Link the enlarged intercostal arteries to erosion of the rib grooves.
questions.why: The narrowing sits beyond the left subclavian artery, so pressure is high above it and low below it, and blood takes detours around the block. The subclavian arteries feed the internal thoracic arteries, which send blood into the anterior intercostal arteries. That blood flows backward through the posterior intercostal arteries into the descending aorta below the narrowing. Over years these intercostal arteries enlarge, become tortuous, and erode the grooves on the lower borders of the ribs. The first two ribs are spared because their posterior intercostal arteries come from the subclavian system rather than the aorta.
whyNot: This is the normal direction of flow in the posterior intercostal arteries. In coarctation the aorta below the narrowing has low pressure, so the flow reverses toward it.
This is normal venous drainage of the chest wall. Coarctation does not raise venous pressure, and the enlarged vessels that notch the ribs are arteries.
Bronchial arteries normally arise from the aorta and carry blood toward the lungs. Large aortopulmonary collaterals matter in pulmonary atresia, and they do not run in the rib grooves.
Correct.

topics: Collateral circulation of the thoracic wall

questions.stem: During surgical repair near the ligamentum arteriosum, the surgeon protects the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks under the aortic arch. On the right side, the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around a vessel derived from which of the following embryonic arteries?
options: Right fourth aortic arch artery
Right third aortic arch artery
Right sixth aortic arch artery
Right second aortic arch artery
approach: Recall that both recurrent laryngeal nerves start out under the sixth arch arteries.
On the right, the distal sixth arch regresses, so the nerve moves up to the next arch artery.
Name the vessel: the right subclavian artery, whose proximal part comes from the fourth arch.
questions.why: Both recurrent laryngeal nerves supply sixth arch muscles and first hook under the sixth arch arteries. On the left, the distal sixth arch artery persists as the ductus arteriosus, so the nerve stays hooked under it, at the ligamentum arteriosum below the aortic arch. On the right, the distal sixth arch artery and the fifth arch disappear, so the nerve moves up and hooks under the next vessel, the right subclavian artery. The proximal right subclavian artery comes from the right fourth arch artery.
whyNot: Correct.
The third arch arteries form the common carotid arteries and the first part of the internal carotid arteries. The nerve does not hook under them.
The distal right sixth arch artery regresses, which is exactly why the right nerve moves up. Only the left sixth arch persists, as the ductus arteriosus.
The second arch arteries largely regress and leave only small vessels such as the stapedial artery. No vessel from them lies in the path of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: Blood can travel from the aorta above the narrowing to the aorta below it by two parallel routes: through the narrowed segment, with a resistance of 3 mm Hg·min/L, and through the collateral network, with a resistance of 6 mm Hg·min/L. Which of the following is the combined resistance between these two points?
options: 1.5 mm Hg·min/L
2 mm Hg·min/L
4.5 mm Hg·min/L
9 mm Hg·min/L
approach: Decide series or parallel: two routes connecting the same two points are in parallel.
Add the reciprocals: 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2.
Invert the result: total resistance is 2, lower than either path alone.
questions.why: For parallel paths, the reciprocals add: 1/R total = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so R total is 2 mm Hg·min/L. Adding a parallel path always lowers total resistance below that of the smallest single path. This is why growing collaterals lessen the pressure drop across a coarctation over time. The same rule explains why each organ can change its own arteriolar tone and flow without forcing the same change on other organs, since the organ beds branch off the aorta in parallel.
whyNot: 1.5 would need a third parallel route or an error in adding the reciprocals.
Correct.
4.5 is the average of the two resistances. An average describes neither a series nor a parallel circuit.
9 is the sum, which applies to resistances in series. These two routes connect the same two points side by side, so they are in parallel.

questions.stem: His bicuspid aortic valve functions normally at this time. Without intervention, which of the following changes in this valve is most likely to develop over the coming decades?
options: Commissural fusion after rheumatic carditis episodes
Myxomatous mitral degeneration with prolapse
Calcific stenosis decades earlier than usual
Sterile vegetations from a hypercoagulable state
approach: Note the anatomy: two aortic leaflets instead of three.
Recall that two leaflets fold abnormally and meet turbulent flow with every beat.
Predict early dystrophic calcification and stenosis, often in the 40s to 60s rather than after 70.
questions.why: A bicuspid aortic valve affects about 1 to 2% of people. Its two leaflets crease abnormally and meet turbulent flow with each beat, so wear and dystrophic calcification start early. Calcific aortic stenosis therefore tends to appear in the 40s to 60s, decades earlier than on a normal three-cusp valve. Other risks include aortic regurgitation, infective endocarditis, and dilation or dissection of the ascending aorta. The valve is linked to Turner syndrome and often occurs with coarctation, as in this patient.
whyNot: Commissural fusion is the lesion of rheumatic heart disease, which follows repeated immune injury after group A streptococcal pharyngitis. It mainly affects the mitral valve and does not arise from a bicuspid valve.
Myxomatous degeneration with prolapse affects the mitral valve, often in connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome. A bicuspid aortic valve does not cause it.
Correct.
Sterile vegetations form in hypercoagulable states such as advanced cancer, a pattern called nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis. Nothing in his case points to a hypercoagulable state.

dx: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia with xanthomas and supravalvular aortic stenosis in a child
case: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of chest pain when she runs. Her parents are first cousins. Physical examination shows yellow-orange nodules over the elbows and knees, flat yellow plaques in the web spaces between the fingers, and thickened Achilles tendons. A grade 3/6 harsh systolic ejection murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border and radiates to the carotid arteries. Fasting laboratory studies show total cholesterol 745 mg/dL (reference less than 170 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol 690 mg/dL (reference less than 110 mg/dL), HDL cholesterol 40 mg/dL (reference greater than 45 mg/dL), and triglycerides 70 mg/dL (reference less than 75 mg/dL). Both parents have LDL cholesterol near 250 mg/dL. Echocardiography shows lipid-rich narrowing of the aorta just above the aortic valve. The diagnosis is homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her LDL cholesterol is about 3 times that of either parent?
options: Two defective LDL receptor alleles nearly abolish LDL uptake
Two defective apolipoprotein E alleles block remnant clearance
One defective LDL receptor allele acts in a dominant negative way
Two defective lipoprotein lipase alleles block VLDL hydrolysis
approach: Compare the levels: parents about twice normal, child about 6 times normal.
Link the pattern to gene dose: one defective LDL receptor allele in each parent, two in the child.
Check the profile: isolated high LDL with normal triglycerides fits an LDL receptor defect.
questions.why: Each parent carries one defective LDL receptor allele, so their livers make about half the normal number of receptors and their LDL is about twice normal. Because the parents are related, she had a higher chance of inheriting two defective alleles. With little or no receptor activity, LDL clearance nearly stops, so LDL is often above 500 mg/dL. Cholesterol then deposits in skin and tendons as xanthomas and in the aortic root and coronary arteries, causing coronary disease in childhood.
whyNot: Correct.
Apo E2 homozygosity causes dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III), with raised remnants and high cholesterol and triglycerides together. Her triglycerides are normal.
A single defective allele explains her parents' moderate elevation. Her far higher level and her parents' consanguinity point to two defective alleles.
Lipoprotein lipase deficiency raises chylomicrons and triglycerides (type I) and causes pancreatitis. It does not cause high LDL with tendon xanthomas.

questions.stem: Her cultured skin fibroblasts bind labeled LDL normally at the cell surface, but almost none of the bound LDL enters the cells. Which of the following steps is most likely defective?
options: Release of LDL from receptors in acidic endosomes
Hydrolysis of cholesteryl esters in lysosomes
Clustering of receptors into clathrin-coated pits
Transport of new receptors from the ER to the Golgi
approach: Note what works: binding at the surface.
Note what fails: entry into the cell.
Place the defect at the step between binding and endocytosis: clustering into clathrin-coated pits.
questions.why: LDL receptors bind apo B-100 at the cell surface and then gather in clathrin-coated pits, guided by a signal in their cytoplasmic tail. The pits pinch off as coated vesicles and carry LDL inside, where the receptor is released and recycled and the LDL goes to lysosomes. If the tail signal is defective, receptors bind LDL but cannot gather in the pits, so LDL stays outside the cell. These internalization-defective mutations are one of several classes of LDL receptor defects.
whyNot: Release of LDL in acidic endosomes happens after the LDL is already inside. A defect here would still bring LDL into the cell.
Lysosomal acid lipase acts on cholesteryl esters after uptake. A defect here would still let LDL enter the cells.
Correct.
Receptors stuck in the ER never reach the surface, so LDL binding itself would be low. Her cells bind LDL normally.

questions.stem: If the narrowing above her aortic valve is not relieved, which of the following changes in her left ventricle is most likely to develop?
options: Eccentric hypertrophy, sarcomeres added in series
Chamber dilation with thinning of the ventricular wall
Asymmetric septal thickening with myofiber disarray
Concentric hypertrophy, sarcomeres added in parallel
approach: Classify the load: obstruction to outflow is a pressure load.
Apply Laplace: higher pressure means higher wall stress, which a thicker wall offsets.
Match a pressure load to concentric hypertrophy with sarcomeres added in parallel.
questions.why: Narrowing at or above the aortic valve forces the left ventricle to generate high systolic pressure to eject blood. By the law of Laplace, high pressure raises wall stress, and the myocytes respond by adding sarcomeres in parallel. The wall thickens while the chamber stays normal or small, which is concentric hypertrophy. The thick wall needs more oxygen and is harder to perfuse, which adds to the exertional angina seen with aortic outflow obstruction.
whyNot: Sarcomeres added in series lengthen the myocytes and enlarge the chamber. That is the response to volume overload, as in aortic or mitral regurgitation.
Dilation with a thin wall is the picture of dilated cardiomyopathy or late failure. It is not the first adaptation to a pressure load.
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with myofiber disarray is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a sarcomere gene disorder. Outflow narrowing does not cause it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Angiography shows severe narrowing at the ostium of the left main coronary artery from aortic root plaque. She has a right-dominant coronary circulation. Which of the following pairs of arteries both receive their blood through this narrowed ostium?
options: Anterior interventricular and posterior interventricular arteries
Anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries
Circumflex and acute marginal arteries
Posterior interventricular and acute marginal arteries
approach: Recall the two branches of the left main coronary artery.
Use dominance: in a right-dominant heart the posterior interventricular artery comes from the right coronary artery.
Choose the pair made only of left main branches.
questions.why: The left main coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus and runs a short course behind the pulmonary trunk. It divides into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery, which runs in the anterior interventricular groove, and the circumflex artery, which runs in the left atrioventricular groove. Together they supply the anterior and lateral walls of the left ventricle and the anterior two-thirds of the septum. In a right-dominant heart, the posterior interventricular artery and the acute marginal artery both come from the right coronary artery.
whyNot: In a right-dominant circulation, the posterior interventricular artery arises from the right coronary artery. It comes from the circumflex only in a left-dominant heart.
Correct.
The acute marginal artery runs along the right border of the heart and is a branch of the right coronary artery.
Both of these are right coronary branches in a right-dominant heart, so neither depends on the left main ostium.

dx: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome (lipoprotein lipase deficiency) with eruptive xanthomas
case: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting for 1 day. He has had episodes of abdominal pain since infancy. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg. Physical examination shows epigastric tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, and crops of small yellow papules with red bases on the buttocks and the extensor surfaces of the arms. Retinal vessels appear pale and creamy. Laboratory studies show lipase 980 U/L (reference 13 to 60 U/L), triglycerides 3,200 mg/dL (reference less than 150 mg/dL), and total cholesterol 310 mg/dL. Plasma stored at 4 °C (39.2 °F) overnight forms a creamy top layer over clear plasma. Lipoprotein lipase activity in postheparin plasma is nearly absent. The diagnosis is familial chylomicronemia syndrome from lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following lipoprotein patterns best explains the appearance of his refrigerated plasma?
options: Excess VLDL with near-normal chylomicrons
Excess chylomicrons and excess VLDL
Excess chylomicrons with near-normal VLDL
Excess IDL and chylomicron remnant particles
approach: Read the tube: creamy top, clear bottom.
Recall that chylomicrons float, while VLDL causes diffuse cloudiness.
Match an isolated chylomicron excess to loss of lipoprotein lipase (type I).
questions.why: Lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium hydrolyzes the triglyceride in chylomicrons and VLDL, with apo C-II as its activator. Without the enzyme, chylomicrons from the diet cannot be cleared and build up to very high levels. Chylomicrons are large and light, so they float to the top as a creamy layer when plasma stands cold. The clear plasma underneath shows that VLDL is not markedly raised. This is the type I pattern, and its main danger is acute pancreatitis.
whyNot: Excess VLDL alone (type IV) makes the whole sample evenly cloudy with no creamy top layer. It comes from overproduction of VLDL by the liver.
Excess chylomicrons and VLDL together (type V) give a creamy layer over a cloudy lower layer. His lower layer is clear.
Correct.

Remnant buildup (type III) comes from apo E2 homozygosity and raises cholesterol and triglycerides about equally. It causes palmar xanthomas and early atherosclerosis, and the sample does not form a separate creamy layer.

questions.stem: Which of the following best traces the path by which dietary triglyceride from his meals reaches the bloodstream?
options: Intestinal capillaries, portal vein, liver sinusoids, hepatic veins
Lacteals, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, left venous angle
Lacteals, cisterna chyli, right lymphatic duct, right venous angle
Lacteals, mesenteric nodes, azygos vein, superior vena cava
approach: Start with the particle: chylomicrons are too large for blood capillaries.
Follow intestinal lymph: lacteals to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct.
End at the left venous angle, where the thoracic duct empties.
questions.why: Enterocytes pack dietary triglyceride into chylomicrons, which are too large to enter blood capillaries. They pass into the lacteals in the villi, then through the intestinal lymph trunks to the cisterna chyli in the upper abdomen. The thoracic duct carries this lymph up through the thorax and empties it at the left venous angle, the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. The right lymphatic duct drains only the right side of the head, neck, and thorax and the right upper limb.
whyNot: Water-soluble nutrients such as glucose, amino acids, and short-chain fatty acids enter intestinal capillaries and the portal vein. Chylomicrons are too large for this route.
Correct.
The right lymphatic duct drains only the right side of the head, neck, and thorax and the right upper limb. Intestinal lymph always joins the thoracic duct.
The azygos vein carries venous blood from the posterior thoracic wall. Lymph from the gut does not drain into it.

questions.stem: Lymph flow in his mesenteric lymphatic vessels rises sharply after a fatty meal. These vessels lie in the mesentery, away from skeletal muscle. Which of the following mainly moves this lymph toward the thoracic duct?
options: Lymphangion contraction between one-way valves
Rising intrathoracic pressure during each inspiration
Compression by contracting nearby skeletal muscle
Colloid osmotic pull of chylomicrons in the lumen
approach: Note the setting: mesenteric vessels with no skeletal muscle nearby.
List the forces that move lymph and remove those that do not apply here.
Choose the intrinsic pump: stretch-triggered contraction of lymphangions with valves.
questions.why: Collecting lymphatic vessels are divided by valves into segments called lymphangions. Each segment has smooth muscle that contracts when filling stretches it, pushing lymph past the valve ahead while the valve behind closes. In the mesentery, where no skeletal muscle surrounds the vessels, this intrinsic pump does most of the work. Rising interstitial fluid and more filling make the pump beat harder, and breathing helps in the thorax because falling intrathoracic pressure during inspiration draws lymph into the thoracic duct.
whyNot: Correct.
Intrathoracic pressure falls during inspiration, and that fall helps draw lymph into the thoracic duct. A rise would oppose flow.
The skeletal muscle pump matters most in the limbs. The stem places these vessels away from skeletal muscle.
Osmotic forces move water across membranes. They cannot push lymph along a vessel in one direction.

questions.stem: His physician explains that despite his very high triglyceride level since infancy, his risk of premature coronary atherosclerosis is not markedly increased. Which of the following best explains this?
options: Chylomicron triglyceride is oxidized before reaching arteries
Chylomicrons carry apo B-100 that blocks scavenger receptors
High triglycerides raise HDL, which clears plaque cholesterol
Chylomicrons are too large to enter the arterial intima
approach: Recall the first step of atherosclerosis: small apo B lipoproteins enter the intima.
Compare particle sizes: chylomicrons are far larger than LDL.
Conclude that chylomicrons rarely reach the intima, so his main risk is pancreatitis.
questions.why: Atherosclerosis starts when LDL and other small apo B particles cross injured endothelium and are trapped in the intima. There they are oxidized and taken up by macrophages through scavenger receptors, forming foam cells and the fatty streak, which later becomes a fibrous plaque. Chylomicrons are far larger than LDL, so they cannot easily cross the endothelium into the intima. Without lipoprotein lipase, few smaller remnants form, so cholesterol delivery into the artery wall stays limited. His main danger is pancreatitis rather than early coronary disease.
whyNot: Lipoproteins are oxidized after they enter the intima, which is the step chylomicrons rarely reach. Plasma triglyceride is not oxidized on the way to the arteries.
Chylomicrons carry apo B-48. Apo B-100 is on VLDL, IDL, and LDL, and it does not block scavenger receptors.
High triglycerides usually lower HDL. A raised HDL is not the reason for his lower risk.
Correct.

dx: Takayasu arteritis with absent radial pulses
case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 4 months of fatigue, night sweats, joint aches, and a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. For 3 weeks, her left arm has ached and tired when she dries her hair. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg in the right arm and 92/60 mm Hg in the left arm. The left radial pulse is absent, and the right radial pulse is weak. Bruits are heard over the left supraclavicular fossa and both carotid arteries. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 68 mm/h (reference 0 to 20 mm/h). MR angiography shows wall thickening of the aortic arch with long, smooth narrowings of the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery. The diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the lower blood pressure in her left arm?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque narrowing the origin of the subclavian
Stenosis from granulomatous arteritis of the vessel wall
Compression of the subclavian artery by a cervical rib
Embolus from the left atrium lodged in the brachial artery
approach: Combine the clues: a young woman, systemic inflammation, and narrowed aortic arch branches.
Recognize a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis.
Link the narrowed left subclavian artery to low left arm pressure.
questions.why: Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of the aorta and its main branches. Inflammation thickens the media and adventitia, and the intima then thickens with fibrosis, producing long, smooth narrowings. When the left subclavian artery narrows, pressure beyond it falls, so the left arm pressure is low and its pulse weak or absent. Fever, night sweats, and a high ESR come from the active inflammation.
whyNot: Atherosclerosis of the subclavian origin is a disease of older adults with vascular risk factors. It does not cause fever, night sweats, or long smooth narrowings of several arch branches in a 24-year-old.
Correct.
A cervical rib compresses the subclavian artery with arm movement. It does not cause fever, a high ESR, or narrowing of the carotid arteries.
An embolus causes sudden ischemia of one limb. It does not explain months of systemic symptoms and narrowing of several arch branches.

questions.stem: Serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are negative, complement levels are normal, and immunofluorescence of an arterial biopsy specimen shows no immune deposits. Which of the following immune mechanisms best explains her vasculitis?
options: Immune complex deposition with complement activation
ANCA activation of neutrophils at the endothelium
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the media
T cell-driven granulomatous inflammation of the wall
approach: Use the negative tests: no ANCA, normal complement, no deposits.
Rule out antibody and immune complex mechanisms.
Assign granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis to the T cell and macrophage group.
questions.why: Vasculitides are grouped by how the immune system injures the vessel. Takayasu and giant cell arteritis are driven by T cells: activated T cells release cytokines that recruit and activate macrophages, which form granulomas with giant cells in the media. No antibody is needed, so ANCA is negative, complement is normal, and immune deposits are absent. Immune complex vasculitis includes polyarteritis nodosa with hepatitis B, IgA vasculitis, and cryoglobulinemia, while ANCA-associated vasculitis includes GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, and EGPA.
whyNot: Immune complex vasculitis often lowers complement and leaves granular deposits of immunoglobulin and C3. Her complement is normal and deposits are absent.
ANCA vasculitis affects small vessels and requires circulating ANCA. Her test is negative, and her disease involves the aorta and its main branches.
IgE and mast cells drive type I hypersensitivity, such as allergy and asthma. They are not the mechanism of large-vessel vasculitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Giant cell arteritis can also involve the aortic arch branches and cause arm claudication, with the same granulomatous histology. Which of the following features of this patient best distinguishes her condition from giant cell arteritis?
options: Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Onset before 50 years of age
Narrowing of the aortic arch branches
approach: List what both diseases share: granulomas, giant cells, a high ESR, and arch branch narrowing.
Find the feature that differs: age at onset.
Note that giant cell arteritis begins after 50, while Takayasu arteritis begins in young adults.
questions.why: Giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis look alike under the microscope, with granulomatous inflammation and giant cells in the media. Both raise the ESR, and both can narrow the aortic arch branches. The most reliable difference is age: giant cell arteritis almost never begins before age 50, while Takayasu arteritis usually begins before 40, often in young Asian women. Giant cell arteritis also favors carotid branches such as the temporal artery, causing headache, jaw claudication, and a risk of blindness, and it is linked to polymyalgia rheumatica.
whyNot: Granulomas with giant cells occur in both diseases, which is why histology cannot separate them.
A high ESR is typical of both diseases during active inflammation.
Correct.
Both diseases can narrow the arch branches. Giant cell arteritis involves the aorta and its branches in a sizable minority of patients.

questions.stem: Narrowing of which of the following single vessels would reduce flow into both her right upper limb and her right common carotid artery?
options: Brachiocephalic trunk
Right subclavian artery
Right internal thoracic artery
Left common carotid artery
approach: Recall the arch branches from right to left.
Find the one vessel that gives rise to both the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
Choose the brachiocephalic trunk.
questions.why: The aortic arch has three branches, from right to left: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery. The brachiocephalic trunk passes up behind the right sternoclavicular joint and divides into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries. A narrowing in the trunk therefore lowers flow to both the right arm and the right side of the head and neck. On the left, the carotid and subclavian arteries arise separately from the arch, so each can be narrowed alone.
whyNot: Correct.
The right subclavian artery supplies the right arm but begins where the right common carotid artery has already branched off. Its narrowing would spare carotid flow.
The internal thoracic artery is a branch of the subclavian artery that runs down the anterior chest wall. It supplies neither the arm nor the carotid artery.
The left common carotid artery arises directly from the arch and supplies the left side of the head and neck. It has no connection to the right arm.

dx: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis with sinusitis, lung nodules, and glomerulonephritis
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of 3 months of nasal stuffiness with bloody crusts, facial pain, and a cough with streaks of blood. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. Physical examination shows ulcerated nasal mucosa and a perforated nasal septum. Chest CT shows several bilateral nodules, some with cavities. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red blood cells, and 2+ protein. Serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL (reference 0.7 to 1.3 mg/dL). Biopsy of the nasal lesion shows necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with vasculitis of small arteries. Kidney biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with few immune deposits. The diagnosis is granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

questions.stem: Testing for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies is positive. Which of the following is the most likely target of these antibodies?
options: Myeloperoxidase
Type IV collagen alpha-3 chain
Phospholipase A2 receptor
Proteinase 3
approach: Recognize the triad: upper airway disease, lung nodules, and glomerulonephritis, with granulomas.
Name the disease: granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Match it to its usual ANCA target, proteinase 3.
questions.why: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis of the upper airway, lungs, and kidneys that forms necrotizing granulomas. Most patients have ANCA against proteinase 3, a serine protease in neutrophil granules, which gives a cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) staining pattern. ANCA bind to primed neutrophils and trigger them to release granule enzymes and reactive oxygen species that damage endothelium. Microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis are usually MPO-ANCA positive, and microscopic polyangiitis lacks granulomas.
whyNot: MPO-ANCA, with a perinuclear pattern, is typical of microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Necrotizing granulomas of the nose and lungs point to GPA.
Antibodies to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen cause anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), with linear IgG on the basement membrane. They are not ANCA and do not cause sinus granulomas.
Antibodies to the phospholipase A2 receptor cause primary membranous nephropathy, which presents with nephrotic syndrome rather than vasculitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Examination of his lower legs shows raised, nonblanching red-purple spots 4 to 8 mm across. Which of the following terms best describes these lesions?
options: Purpura
Petechiae
Ecchymoses
Hematomas
approach: Use the blanching test: no blanching means the blood is outside the vessels.
Measure the lesions: 4 to 8 mm.
Match the size to the term: purpura.
questions.why: Nonblanching spots mean red cells have left the vessels, because pressure cannot push extravasated blood away. Skin hemorrhages are named by size: petechiae are 1 to 2 mm, purpura are 3 mm or more, and ecchymoses are larger bruises over about 1 to 2 cm. In small-vessel vasculitis, inflamed and damaged venules leak blood into the dermis, and the inflammation makes the spots raised, so they are called palpable purpura.
whyNot: Correct.
Petechiae are pinpoint hemorrhages of 1 to 2 mm, typical of low platelet counts or capillary injury. These lesions are larger.
Ecchymoses are larger, flat bruises over about 1 to 2 cm, as after blunt trauma.
A hematoma is a collection of clotted blood within a tissue or space that forms a mass. It is not a small skin spot.

questions.stem: Blood flow to the poorly ventilated lung tissue around his nodules is reduced. Which of the following mechanisms most directly causes this local reduction?
options: Sympathetic alpha-1 constriction of pulmonary arterioles
Alveolar hypoxia constricting nearby pulmonary arterioles
Myogenic constriction of arterioles in response to stretch
Endothelin release from inflamed small pulmonary veins
approach: Note the setting: poorly ventilated alveoli with a low PO2.
Recall that the pulmonary bed is the one bed where hypoxia constricts arterioles.
Choose hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which matches perfusion to ventilation.
questions.why: In most systemic beds, low O2 dilates arterioles to raise flow. In the lung, low alveolar PO2 does the opposite and constricts the small pulmonary arteries next to the hypoxic alveoli. This hypoxic vasoconstriction is the main local control of pulmonary blood flow, and it shifts blood toward better-ventilated regions to keep ventilation and perfusion matched. Other beds have different main controls: metabolites in the heart and exercising muscle, PCO2 in the brain, and sympathetic nerves in the skin.
whyNot: Sympathetic nerves have only a small effect on pulmonary vessels, and they act on the whole lung instead of one poorly ventilated region.
Correct.
Myogenic responses matter most in the kidney and brain, where they buffer changes in pressure. Pulmonary vessels respond mainly to alveolar O2.
Endothelin contributes to pulmonary hypertension, but regional flow is set at the small arteries and arterioles, and the trigger here is low alveolar O2.

topics: Local control of blood flow by organ

questions.stem: Two days later, he develops diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and needs mechanical ventilation with high positive end-expiratory pressure. He is hypotensive, and the head of his bed is raised to 45 degrees. His uppermost lung units are ventilated but receive no blood flow. Which of the following pressure relationships exists in these units?
options: Pulmonary arterial pressure above alveolar pressure
Pulmonary venous pressure above alveolar pressure
Alveolar pressure above pulmonary arterial pressure
Interstitial pressure above pulmonary venous pressure
approach: Note the setting: low arterial pressure, positive airway pressure, and an upright chest.
Recall that zone 1 means alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure, collapsing the capillaries.
Place zone 1 at the top of the lung, where arterial pressure is lowest.
questions.why: When the chest is upright, the weight of the blood column makes pulmonary arterial pressure lowest at the top of the lung, while alveolar pressure is about the same everywhere. If alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure, the capillaries collapse and no blood flows. This is zone 1, which is alveolar dead space with a V/Q ratio near infinity. Zone 1 is rare in health, but it appears when arterial pressure falls, as in hemorrhage or shock, or when alveolar pressure rises, as with positive pressure ventilation. This patient has both.
whyNot: Arterial pressure above alveolar pressure keeps capillaries open for at least part of the cycle. That describes zone 2 or zone 3, where blood flows.
Venous pressure above alveolar pressure describes zone 3 at the lung base, where flow is continuous and highest.
Correct.
High interstitial pressure at the very base (sometimes called zone 4) lowers flow by squeezing extra-alveolar vessels. It does not describe ventilated top units with no flow.

dx: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) in a child
case: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a rash on his legs, swollen ankles, and crampy abdominal pain for 4 days. Two weeks ago he had a sore throat and runny nose. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows raised, nonblanching purple spots on the buttocks and the backs of the legs and tender swelling of both ankles. A stool test for occult blood is positive. Platelet count is 310,000/mm3 (reference 150,000 to 400,000/mm3), and prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times are normal. Urinalysis shows 15 red blood cells per high-power field (reference 0 to 2) and 1+ protein. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis of small dermal vessels with IgA deposits on immunofluorescence. The diagnosis is IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura).

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy is performed because the hematuria persists for several months. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Mesangial deposits of IgA-containing immune complexes
Subepithelial humps of IgG and C3 on the basement membrane
Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
Crescents with few or no immune deposits
approach: Note the skin biopsy: IgA deposits in small vessels.
Link IgA vasculitis to the kidney: the same IgA complexes lodge in the mesangium.
Pick mesangial IgA deposits, the lesion of IgA nephropathy.
questions.why: IgA vasculitis is an immune complex small-vessel vasculitis. Poorly galactosylated IgA1 forms complexes that deposit in small vessel walls of the skin, gut, and joints and in the glomerular mesangium. The kidney lesion matches IgA nephropathy, with mesangial IgA and C3 on immunofluorescence. It often follows an upper respiratory infection, and most children recover fully.
whyNot: Correct.
Subepithelial humps of IgG and C3 are typical of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. It does not cause purpura or IgA deposits.
Linear IgG marks anti-GBM disease, caused by antibodies to type IV collagen.
Crescents with few deposits are typical of ANCA-associated vasculitis. IgA vasculitis has prominent IgA deposits.

questions.stem: Polyarteritis nodosa can also cause abdominal pain and kidney involvement. Which of the following features of this boy's illness best distinguishes it from polyarteritis nodosa?
options: Abdominal pain from mesenteric vessel inflammation
Small-vessel involvement with IgA immune deposits
Kidney involvement with microscopic hematuria
Negative test for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
approach: List the overlap: abdominal pain, kidney involvement, and a negative ANCA test.
Recall vessel size: polyarteritis nodosa affects medium arteries and spares small vessels.
Pick the feature unique to IgA vasculitis: small vessels with IgA deposits.
questions.why: Polyarteritis nodosa is a transmural necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries, such as the renal and mesenteric arteries. Lesions of different ages sit side by side, microaneurysms and infarcts form, the lungs are spared, and many cases are linked to hepatitis B. Because it spares capillaries, venules, and glomeruli, it does not cause palpable purpura from leaky venules or glomerulonephritis with IgA deposits. Both diseases can cause abdominal pain and kidney findings, and both are ANCA negative.
whyNot: Both diseases inflame mesenteric vessels and cause abdominal pain, so this feature does not separate them.
Correct.
Polyarteritis nodosa also involves the kidney, through renal artery inflammation, infarcts, and hypertension, and hematuria can occur in both.
Polyarteritis nodosa is ANCA negative too, so a negative ANCA test does not separate them.

questions.stem: The kidneys receive a large blood flow for their size, which brings many circulating immune complexes to the glomeruli. Which of the following best describes the kidneys' share of resting cardiac output and their oxygen extraction?
options: About 5%, with high O2 extraction
About 15%, with moderate O2 extraction
About 20%, with low O2 extraction
About 25%, with high O2 extraction
approach: Recall the resting distribution of cardiac output by organ.
Link flow to purpose: renal flow serves filtration, so O2 extraction is low.
Choose about 20% with low O2 extraction.
questions.why: At rest the kidneys receive about 20% of cardiac output, roughly 1 L/min, though they make up less than 1% of body weight. This flow serves filtration, not metabolism, so the kidneys extract only a small fraction of the O2 delivered and renal venous blood stays well oxygenated. The heart is the opposite: it receives about 5% of cardiac output and extracts about 70% of the O2, so it must raise flow to meet any added demand. The brain receives about 15% with moderate extraction, and the gut and liver together receive about 25%.
whyNot: About 5% with high extraction describes the heart, which removes most of the delivered O2 even at rest.
About 15% with moderate extraction describes the brain.
Correct.
About 25% is the combined share of the gut and liver, whose O2 extraction at rest is moderate. Neither part fits the kidneys.

questions.stem: In the same clinic, a 3-year-old girl has had 6 days of fever to 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, cracked red lips, a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous rash on the trunk, swelling of the hands and feet, and a 2-cm cervical lymph node. Her vasculitis places which of the following structures at greatest risk?
options: Glomerular capillaries, through crescent formation
Mesenteric arterioles, through bowel infarction
Retinal arteries, through sudden occlusion
Coronary arteries, through aneurysm formation
approach: Recognize Kawasaki disease from 5 or more days of fever plus mucocutaneous signs and a large cervical node.
Recall that it is a medium-vessel vasculitis that favors the coronary arteries.
Predict coronary aneurysm as the key complication.
questions.why: Fever for 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, swelling of the hands and feet, and cervical lymphadenopathy in a young child is Kawasaki disease. It is a medium-vessel vasculitis with a strong preference for the coronary arteries. Inflammation weakens the arterial wall and can form coronary aneurysms in up to about a quarter of untreated children, and these can later thrombose and cause myocardial infarction. Early treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin lowers this risk.
whyNot: Glomerular injury is the main threat in IgA vasculitis and ANCA-associated vasculitis. Kidney involvement in her condition is uncommon and mild.
Bowel ischemia occurs in IgA vasculitis and polyarteritis nodosa. It is not the key complication of her condition.
Sudden loss of vision from arterial occlusion is the feared result of giant cell arteritis in adults over 50.
Correct.

dx: Kaposi sarcoma in a heart transplant recipient on immunosuppression
case: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of purple spots on his legs for 2 months. He was born in southern Italy. Fourteen months ago he received a heart transplant for dilated cardiomyopathy, and he takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows several violet plaques and nodules on both lower legs and one on the hard palate. Biopsy of a leg nodule shows spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated red blood cells, and the spindle cells stain for human herpesvirus 8 latency-associated nuclear antigen. HIV testing is negative. The diagnosis is transplant-associated Kaposi sarcoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best predicts the course of his tumor?
options: Stays indolent for decades with no change in treatment
Regresses only after antiretroviral therapy restores CD4 counts
Often regresses when immunosuppression is reduced
Rarely regresses because HHV-8 DNA integrates into host DNA
approach: Identify the form: Kaposi sarcoma in an HIV-negative transplant recipient taking immunosuppressive drugs.
Link tumor growth to weak T cell control of HHV-8.
Predict that lowering immunosuppression often makes the lesions regress.
questions.why: Kaposi sarcoma arises from HHV-8 infected spindle cells, and its growth depends on weak T cell control of the virus. In transplant recipients, the drugs that prevent rejection also weaken this control, so lesions often appear within the first 1 to 2 years. When immunosuppression is reduced, many lesions shrink or disappear. The classic form in older men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent stays indolent on the legs, the endemic African form can involve lymph nodes in children, and the AIDS form improves when antiretroviral therapy restores immunity.
whyNot: A slow course over decades on the lower legs describes classic Kaposi sarcoma in older men without immune suppression. His tumor is driven by drug-induced immune suppression.
Antiretroviral therapy helps AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma. He is HIV negative.
Correct.
HHV-8 persists in cells as an episome and does not integrate into host DNA. Restored T cell control can still shrink the lesions.

questions.stem: Three months after the transplant, a routine endomyocardial biopsy showed a dense interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes with focal myocyte necrosis. Staining for C4d in the capillaries was negative. Which of the following mechanisms best explains that biopsy finding?
options: Preformed host antibodies binding donor endothelium
Donor T cells in the graft attacking host tissue
Intimal smooth muscle proliferation narrowing coronary arteries
Host CD8+ T cells attacking cells that display donor MHC
approach: Note the timing: 3 months after transplant.
Note the pattern: lymphocytes with myocyte necrosis and negative C4d.
Match these to acute cellular rejection by host T cells against donor MHC.
questions.why: Acute cellular rejection usually appears in the first months after transplant. Host T cells recognize donor MHC molecules, either directly on donor cells or after host antigen-presenting cells process them. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells kill donor myocytes, and CD4+ T cells release cytokines that recruit more inflammatory cells, giving a lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte damage. Negative C4d argues against antibody-mediated rejection, in which donor-specific antibodies bind capillary endothelium and fix complement.
whyNot: Preformed antibodies cause hyperacute rejection within minutes to hours, with thrombosis of graft vessels. This biopsy was taken at 3 months and showed lymphocytes.
Donor T cells attacking the host is graft-versus-host disease, mainly a problem after bone marrow transplant. It targets the host's skin, gut, and liver.
Intimal proliferation in graft coronary arteries is cardiac allograft vasculopathy, the chronic form of rejection that develops over years.
Correct.

questions.stem: During a treadmill test, his heart rate rises only slowly over the first several minutes of exercise and stays elevated for several minutes after he stops. Which of the following best explains the slow early rise?
options: Graft denervation, so the rate follows blood catecholamines
Loss of central command signals from the motor cortex
Blunted muscle metaboreceptor reflexes from immunosuppressant use
Reduced beta-1 receptor density from chronic rejection
approach: Recall the normal early exercise response: vagal withdrawal within seconds, then sympathetic drive.
Note that a transplanted heart has no cardiac nerves.
Conclude that the rate can rise only as circulating catecholamines build up.
questions.why: In a normal heart, exercise starts with central command and signals from muscle mechanoreceptors that withdraw vagal tone within seconds, so heart rate jumps at once. Rising sympathetic drive then adds more over the next minutes. A transplanted heart has no vagal or sympathetic nerves, so neither signal reaches its sinoatrial node. The rate rises only as epinephrine from the adrenal medulla and norepinephrine spilling over from sympathetic nerves elsewhere build up in blood, which takes minutes, and it falls slowly as they are cleared.
whyNot: Correct.
Central command still starts in his brain and still raises his blood pressure and breathing. Its signal cannot reach the heart because the cardiac nerves were cut.
His muscle reflexes are intact, since his muscles and spinal cord are normal. These reflexes also act through cardiac nerves, which the graft lacks.
The graft still responds to circulating catecholamines through its beta-1 receptors, which is how his rate eventually rises. Rejection does not explain the delay.

questions.stem: His resting pulse has been 90 to 100/min since the transplant. Which of the following best explains his fast resting heart rate?
options: More norepinephrine released from cardiac sympathetic nerves
Loss of acetylcholine effects that flatten the phase 4 slope
Reduced L-type Ca2+ current raising the threshold potential
Greater K+ conductance making repolarization faster
approach: Recall that resting heart rate is the intrinsic nodal rate slowed by vagal tone.
Note that the transplanted heart has no vagal input.
Conclude that phase 4 depolarizes faster without acetylcholine, so the rate rises to the intrinsic level.
questions.why: Sinoatrial node cells drift toward threshold during phase 4 through the funny current carried by HCN channels and then T-type Ca2+ current, and L-type Ca2+ channels produce the upstroke. At rest, vagal acetylcholine opens K+ channels and reduces the funny current, which flattens the phase 4 slope and holds the rate near 60 to 80/min. After transplant, the vagus no longer reaches the node, so it fires at its intrinsic rate of about 90 to 110/min. Norepinephrine would steepen the slope, but the graft has no sympathetic nerves either.
whyNot: The graft has no sympathetic nerves, so it receives no norepinephrine from cardiac nerves at rest.
Correct.
Less L-type Ca2+ current would make the upstroke harder to trigger and slow the rate.
More K+ conductance hyperpolarizes nodal cells and slows the rate. That is what acetylcholine does, and its loss has the opposite effect.

dx: Enterococcal endocarditis of the mitral valve after urinary tract instrumentation in an older man
case: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician because of 4 weeks of fevers, night sweats, fatigue, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. Six weeks ago he had cystoscopy and transurethral resection of the prostate. An echocardiogram 2 years ago showed mild thickening of the mitral leaflets with trace regurgitation. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 126/70 mm Hg. A new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex and radiates to the left axilla. There are splinter hemorrhages under several fingernails. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL (reference 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL). Three of 3 blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecalis. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 1.2-cm vegetation on the anterior mitral leaflet with moderate mitral regurgitation. The diagnosis is subacute enterococcal endocarditis of the mitral valve.

questions.stem: The next day, small, tender, raised red-purple nodules appear on the pads of two fingers. Which of the following best explains these lesions?
options: Septic microemboli forming painless hemorrhagic macules
Linear capillary rupture under the nail plate
Low platelet count causing bleeding into the dermis
Immune complex deposition with local inflammation
approach: Name the lesion: tender nodules on the finger pads are Osler nodes.
Recall the classic mechanism: immune complexes, which explains the pain.
Contrast them with painless Janeway lesions from septic emboli.
questions.why: Tender nodules on the finger or toe pads in endocarditis are Osler nodes. They are classically explained by immune complexes, formed during a long-running bacteremia, that deposit in small vessels and cause local inflammation, which is why they hurt. They are more typical of subacute endocarditis, caused by less virulent organisms such as viridans streptococci and enterococci on previously damaged valves. Janeway lesions are painless flat macules on the palms and soles from septic microemboli and are more typical of acute endocarditis from Staphylococcus aureus.
whyNot: Septic microemboli that form painless, flat hemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles are Janeway lesions. His lesions are tender, raised nodules on the finger pads.
Linear bleeding under the nails produces splinter hemorrhages, which he already has. They are flat streaks, not tender nodules on the finger pads.
Thrombocytopenia causes flat, painless petechiae. It does not form tender nodules on the finger pads.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how the organism came to form a vegetation on his mitral valve?
options: Bacteria spread from the prostate through pelvic lymphatics
Bacteria invaded intact endothelium with pore-forming toxins
Bacteria adhered to fibrin and platelets on injured endothelium
Bacteria were carried to the valve inside circulating monocytes
approach: Note the setting: urinary tract instrumentation in an older man, a classic source of enterococcal bacteremia.
Note the prior valve damage that creates a fibrin-platelet deposit.
Link the two: circulating bacteria stick to the deposit and grow into a vegetation.
questions.why: Urinary tract procedures such as transurethral resection of the prostate can release enterococci and other urinary and gut flora into the blood. A valve with prior damage, here a thickened leaflet with regurgitant flow, develops small sterile deposits of fibrin and platelets on its injured surface. Circulating enterococci stick to these deposits, multiply, and are covered by more fibrin and platelets, which shields them from neutrophils. Enterococci are a leading cause of endocarditis after genitourinary and gastrointestinal procedures, often in older men.
whyNot: Pelvic lymph drains to iliac nodes and does not carry bacteria straight to a heart valve. Endocarditis starts from bacteria in the blood.
Highly virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus can attack normal valves in acute endocarditis. Enterococci are less virulent and need a damaged surface.
Correct.
Valves are seeded by free bacteria in the blood that stick to a fibrin-platelet deposit. Carriage inside monocytes is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Transesophageal echocardiography also shows that several chordae tendineae of the anterior mitral leaflet have ruptured. These chordae arise from which of the following?
options: Anterolateral papillary muscle only
Anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles
Posteromedial papillary muscle only
Anterior, posterior, and septal papillary muscles
approach: Recall that the left ventricle has two papillary muscles.
Recall that each muscle sends chordae to both mitral leaflets.
Conclude that the anterior leaflet receives chordae from both muscles.
questions.why: The mitral valve has an anterior and a posterior leaflet, and the left ventricle has two papillary muscles, anterolateral and posteromedial. Each papillary muscle sends chordae to both leaflets, to the half of each leaflet on its own side. During systole the papillary muscles contract and the chordae keep the leaflets from swinging back into the left atrium. Rupture of chordae lets part of a leaflet flail, which worsens regurgitation. The mitral valve is heard best at the apex.
whyNot: The anterolateral papillary muscle supplies the lateral halves of both leaflets. The anterior leaflet also receives chordae from the posteromedial muscle.
Correct.
The posteromedial papillary muscle supplies the medial halves of both leaflets. It is not the only source for the anterior leaflet.
Anterior, posterior, and septal papillary muscles belong to the right ventricle and the tricuspid valve.

questions.stem: An S3 is also heard at the apex. Which of the following best explains this sound in his condition?
options: Rapid early filling from a large left atrial volume
Atrial contraction into a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle
Sudden tensing of chordae under a prolapsing leaflet
Delayed closure of the pulmonic valve in inspiration
approach: Place the sound: an S3 occurs in early diastole during rapid filling.
Link mitral regurgitation to extra left atrial volume with each beat.
Conclude that rapid emptying of the overloaded atrium into the ventricle makes the S3.
questions.why: In mitral regurgitation, the left atrium receives both the normal pulmonary venous return and the regurgitant jet with each beat. In early diastole this enlarged atrial volume rushes into the left ventricle, and the sudden slowing of this flow against the ventricular wall produces an S3. The S3 reflects volume overload of the left atrium and ventricle. The holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla comes from the regurgitant jet itself.
whyNot: Correct.
Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle makes an S4, heard late in diastole with pressure overload such as hypertension or aortic stenosis.
Sudden tensing of chordae under a prolapsing leaflet makes a midsystolic click, which occurs in systole.
Delayed pulmonic closure splits S2 at the end of systole. An S3 comes after S2, in early diastole.
